item.title: [ADWEEK] Paid and Earned Media Need Couples Counseling

item.content:encoded:
Almost every relationship manual ever written can agree on this core principle: Before you can fix anything, you must truly see each other.
Paid and earned media have been living in the same house for decades without ever really seeing each other. And the moment when that didn’t matter much is over. They’ve never been more interdependent.
The ground has moved under us
The media fragmentation story is well established, and still being written every day. The path and face of influence is perpetually shapeshifting as micro communities form, taking inspiration from a growing and changing world of influencers and creators. And, of course, content discovery has fundamentally changed.
When Muck Rack analyzed more than 25 million links cited by ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini, earned media accounted for 84% of citations. Paid and advertorial content accounted for three-tenths of 1%.
Some are falling into the trap of citation chasing. But beyond a temporary blip, the machines won’t reward citation farming. They’ll reward the accumulated result of being a brand that shows up with something worth discussing.
The notable thing about this moment is not that earned finally has the receipts. It’s that everyone is now saying so—the analysts, the vendors, the Cannes stages—and almost everyone is saying it from their own side of the bed, which is exactly how couples stay stuck.
The numbers will change, for sure. The AI platforms will monetize—native placements, sponsored citations, and licensing deals. When that happens, true partnership becomes even more important.
The relationship reset starts with understanding
Let’s be honest—it’s hardly surprising that the earned-side practitioner is arguing earned deserves a better position. But the more passionate case is being made by clients. The pressure to drive growth is big and the dull tax is even bigger. Paid dollars running parallel to cultural moments instead of extending them, brands invisible in AI answers—this adds up to missed opportunities and underleveraged investment.
Some in the comms industry are using this moment to declare independence—drop the P altogether, an “ESO” model with paid cast as beside-the-point. This is, quite simply, naïve. Dropping the P doesn’t make paid less important; it makes the model incomplete.
Paid delivers a guarantee of both sheer volume and precision earned alone cannot. But earned as the ignition, paid as the fuel, that’s how a fandom fire spreads. Or a paid-first campaign, authoring and embedding a brand identity and idea, the cultural script that earned can build authentic and enduring moments around. Exquisite interdependence. Earned-only is a smaller idea than this moment deserves. One that’s not grounded in respect or reality.
But the misunderstanding runs both ways: Earned expertise is just as opaque from the paid side. What it takes to land a story and shape a story arc so it matters to those the brand is trying to reach—captures their attention, earns their advocacy, prompts a reaction. It’s strategy that considers the flow of influence, how a story starts and how it syndicates, choreographing every element with intention.
Two disciplines. Each holding something the other genuinely needs. That’s not a channel-mix problem. That’s a relationship problem.
What’s actually keeping them apart
The disconnect between paid and earned isn’t just a matter of mindset. It’s built into how the disciplines are structured, staffed, and measured.
The fluency gap. Each side’s blind spot is the other’s entire expertise. Both are functionally illiterate in the other’s language.
The buying structure. Paid media and communications are bought separately—different budgets, different buyers, different procurement tracks.
The measurement question. Standard attribution models were built for a different media era. The work of bringing earned and AI visibility signals into them is underway but genuinely early. That makes this a year for attribution model innovation. The measurement question is the million-dollar question. To work together well, we need to understand each other better and, importantly, evaluate our collective impact more comprehensively.
What progress starts to look like in practice
Closing these gaps requires more than a shared belief in integration. It calls for changes to how teams build expertise across disciplines and demonstrate the value of their combined efforts.
An exchange program that produces hybrid strategists. Earned strategists embedded in media planning; paid strategists inside earned planning rooms. The mission: talent fluent in both disciplines.
Evolving measurement. Building earned into attribution models as an engine variable in the CFO-grade language the model should already speak. The focus: forecasting collective paid and earned impact with real precision, using paid’s certainty to underwrite earned’s variance.
A word on creative: At the heart of this marriage is a commitment to earned-driven creative—ideas conceived to be talked about, cited, and carried, with scale planned beside them. That deserves its own piece (and its own counseling session).
The industry has spent two years aligning on why earned matters. The work is how two disciplines that grew up misunderstanding each other learn to operate as genuine partners inside real budgets, real org charts, real measurement systems.
—
Joy Farber Kolo is chief innovation and integration officer at Weber Shandwick, the premier earned-first communications and consulting agency partnering with nearly half the Fortune 100.
Jonathan Rigby is global chief strategy officer at Omnicom Media, where he leads the strategy craft across Initiative, UM, OMD, PHD, and Hearts United.

item.content:encoded:
U.S. Senator Dave McCormick (Republican-Pennsylvania), a close ally of U.S. President Donald Trump, stated that the South Korea-U.S. alliance is in the process of being "reset," describing it as couples counseling rather than a divorce.
According to the U.S. think tank Hudson Institute on October 18 (local time), McCormick made the remarks during a conversation held in Washington, D.C., on October 16 with Mike Gallagher, former chairman of the House Select Committee on the Chinese Communist Party.
"We are resetting the relationship," McCormick explained. "When you reset a relationship, feelings get hurt and friction occurs."
"Even in a marriage, sometimes the balance gets out of sync, leading one side to tell the other that adjustments are needed," he emphasized, adding that the South Korea-U.S. relationship is "going through couples counseling, not getting a divorce."
He added, "We need more from our Asian allies. The relationship was imbalanced, and they acknowledge that too," and expressed his belief that "we are on the path to a much deeper and stronger relationship."
McCormick recently returned to the United States after visiting Japan and South Korea.
During his trip to South Korea, he visited the Demilitarized Zone (DMZ) and Hanwha Ocean's Geoje shipyard.
He also met with Foreign Minister Cho Hyun and Defense Minister Kang Shin-chul.
Citing the massive investment pledges in the U.S. made by both South Korea and Japan as prime examples of the alliance realignment, McCormick noted, "I heard no controversy (during our meetings in Korea). The conversations were entirely focused on where to invest that capital and how to utilize it."
Mentioning South Korea's pledge to purchase USD 25 billion worth of U.S. military equipment and its plans to increase the defense budget, he evaluated, "We haven't reached the necessary level yet, but we are moving in a direction that aligns with bearing our fair share."
McCormick argued that the United States and its allies must innovate technology faster than China and produce more defense materiel in the long run, asserting, "We must train, plan, and fight with our allies as a single military force and a single military capability."
"If we get this right, China will look across the Taiwan Strait every morning and conclude, 'Not today,'" he said.
